docs.t: AI for small business in New Zealand: What AI can realistically do for a small business
docs.a: Picture a builder at nine o'clock on a weeknight. The kids are in bed, dinner's been eaten, and there are three quotes to write up from site visits earlier in the day. The notes are a mix of scribbles, photos on the phone and a measurement or two remembered on the drive home. That's where most people first wonder whether AI could help. And often it can, but not in the way the headlines suggest. For a small business, AI is rarely a robot that runs the place. It's a tool that reads untidy information, makes sense of it and prepares a first draft for you to check. In that builder's case, a two-minute voice memo after each visit could become a priced draft quote, using their own rates and materials list. They still read it, adjust anything that looks off and decide whether to send it. What disappears is the typing. This guide is for owners who want to use AI sensibly: where it earns its place, where it doesn't, and how to try it without putting your customers or your reputation at risk. AI and automation aren't the same thing. Automation follows fixed rules: when this happens, do that. AI copes with the messy parts, such as understanding a rushed email or a voice memo. Most useful systems use both, with plain automation doing most of the work and AI helping at one or two steps. Our automation glossary explains the other terms you'll hear.
docs.x: AI for small business in New Zealand

docs.t: AI for small business in New Zealand: What AI is good at, and what it isn't
docs.a: Modern AI tools, such as ChatGPT, Claude, Google Gemini and Microsoft Copilot, are built on large language models. They've learned patterns from a huge amount of text, which lets them understand everyday language and write clear replies, summaries and drafts. That makes them strong at some jobs and weak at others: AI is usually good at AI is usually weak at Reading emails, voice memos, photos and handwriting. Knowing facts about your business it hasn't been given. Pulling out details such as names, dates, materials and amounts. Doing exactly the same thing, word for word, every time. Drafting replies, quotes, file notes and summaries. Judgement calls, such as pricing a tricky job or calming an upset customer. Understanding questions written in different ways, or in other languages. Knowing when it's wrong. It can sound confident and still be mistaken. That last point matters most. When an AI tool states something that sounds right but is wrong or made up, it's called a hallucination. A drafted reply might quote opening hours you don't actually keep, or a price you stopped charging last year. That's the main reason a person should check AI-written work before it reaches a customer.
docs.x: AI for small business in New Zealand

docs.t: AI for small business in New Zealand: Practical ways AI can help a small NZ business
docs.a: Most of the useful work falls into a few familiar areas. You don't need all of them. One is plenty to start with. Turning notes and voice memos into quotes. For trades and other on-site businesses, the gap between the site visit and the written quote is often where the evenings go. AI can turn a voice memo, site notes or photos into a draft quote using your rates and wording, ready for you to check. Our guide to automating quotes and invoices walks through how this works. Answering the same customer questions. Opening hours, prices, availability, parking, how to book. An AI assistant can answer these on your website or by email, working only from answers you've approved, and pass anything else to a person. Our guide to AI customer replies for small business covers how to build the answer library and when to hand over. Reading emails, receipts and documents. A supplier invoice in your inbox can be read and turned into a draft bill in Xero for you to approve. A booking request can be read and the details pulled out, ready to add to your calendar. This is AI doing the reading, and plain automation doing the filing. File notes and summaries. An adviser's client call can become a draft file note to check and save. A long email thread can become a short summary of what was agreed. These save time without anything going straight out to a customer. Review replies you approve. AI can draft a reply to each Google review that mentions what the customer actually said, so you approve, edit or skip it from your phone instead of writing every one from scratch. Working across languages. New Zealand businesses serve customers who speak many languages. AI can usually understand a message in one language and reply in the same one, drawing on information written in English. For anything precise, such as prices, terms or health instructions, have a fluent speaker check a sample first.
docs.x: AI for small business in New Zealand

docs.t: AI for small business in New Zealand: What to automate with AI, and what to keep human
docs.a: A simple rule of thumb: if a new staff member could do it correctly on their first day from a printed sheet, AI can probably prepare it. If it needs experience, judgement or authority, it should stay with a person. Good candidates for AI usually: Happen every week, the same way each time. Start with messy input, such as an email, memo, photo or form. End in a draft that's quick to check. Don't cause real harm if a draft needs fixing before it goes out. Keep these with a person, with AI preparing the ground at most: Money decisions. Discounts, refunds, disputes and custom pricing. Complaints and unhappy customers. A calm, personal reply is worth far more than a fast one. Advice. Health, legal, financial or anything a customer might rely on. Decisions about people. Hiring, rosters that affect someone's pay, or anything about a staff member's performance. Anything public that sounds like a promise. Review replies, for example, should never admit fault or offer compensation without a person deciding. AI drafts, people decide. Wherever money, health information or a complaint is involved, set things up so AI prepares the work and a person approves it. Routine messages, such as booking confirmations, can often go straight out once you've seen them working.
docs.x: AI for small business in New Zealand

docs.t: AI for small business in New Zealand: Getting started with AI: one task at a time
docs.a: The most common mistake is starting too big. "Let's use AI across the business" tends to become a project nobody finishes. One task, done properly, tells you far more. List the repetitive work. Ask whoever does the admin what they type, copy, chase and answer every week. Our guide on choosing what to automate first has prompts to get the list going. Time it for one normal week. A rough tally on your phone is enough. Without a starting figure, you can't tell whether AI saved anything. Pick one task with an easy-to-check result. A drafted reply or a draft quote is easier to check than a decision. Write down what good looks like. For example: "each review gets a draft reply in our voice within the hour, and nothing is posted until I approve it". Give it the right information. Your prices, policies, wording and no-go topics. AI works from what it's given, and fills gaps with guesses if you let it. Run it alongside the old way. Check its work on real jobs for long enough to trust it, then switch the manual version off. Measure and decide. Compare the time against your starting week. Then decide whether to keep it, adjust it or try a different task. Most first steps use tools you already pay for, such as Microsoft 365, Google Workspace and Xero. New software should be the exception, not the starting point.
docs.x: AI for small business in New Zealand

docs.t: AI for small business in New Zealand: The risks of AI, and how to manage them
docs.a: None of these is a reason to avoid AI. They're reasons to set it up with care. Wrong answers. AI can misread a memo or invent a detail. Tell it to work only from the information you've given it, to hand over rather than guess, and have a person check drafts, especially in the first few weeks. Out-of-date information. If your prices or hours change and nobody updates what the AI works from, it will keep giving the old answer. Give one person the job of keeping it current. Staff using free tools on their own. Someone pasting a customer's details into a free AI tool to "tidy up an email" may be sending personal information somewhere you haven't checked. Agree which tools are approved and what can go into them. A messy process made faster. If everyone does a job differently, agree one way of working first. AI won't fix an unsettled process. Losing control of your setup. Make sure anything built for you sits in your own accounts, with logins you own, so you keep it if you change provider. Customers not knowing. Be upfront when a customer is talking to an automated assistant, and make a real person easy to reach.
docs.x: AI for small business in New Zealand

docs.t: AI for small business in New Zealand: AI and privacy: what to check first
docs.a: General information, not legal advice. For anything specific to your business, check the guidance from the Office of the Privacy Commissioner or talk to a lawyer. Customer messages, booking details, staff records and client files are usually personal information under the Privacy Act 2020, New Zealand's main privacy law. Using AI doesn't change the rules, but it does add one extra question: does the provider use what you send it to train its models? With some free or consumer versions, it may. With many business plans there are settings or terms that keep your data out of training, but check rather than assume. Before customer or staff information goes into any AI tool, find out: Is our data used for training? Get the answer from the provider's terms or settings, not from a sales page. Where is it processed and stored, and for how long? Many tools process data overseas. That isn't automatically a problem, but you stay responsible for it. Who at the provider can see it? And under what circumstances. Do we need to send personal details at all? Often a summary or draft works just as well with names and contact details removed. Who checks the output? Anything sent to a customer, or used to make a decision about a person, should be checked by someone. When we build AI automations, the data we store for clients is hosted in New Zealand or Australia and never used to train anyone's AI model. Only Ambs works on client projects and sees client data, and the AI tools we use run on business plans that don't train on it. Other tools in the chain, such as your email or accounting software, have their own hosting, so they belong on your checklist too. Our guide to the Privacy Act 2020 and automation has a fuller checklist.
docs.x: AI for small business in New Zealand

docs.t: AI for small business in New Zealand: Questions to ask before you pay for an AI tool
docs.a: Whether you're buying a ready-made AI product or asking someone to build something for you, these questions help separate the useful from the hype: Which of our tasks will it do, and how many hours a week do those take now? What information does it work from, and who keeps that up to date? What happens when it doesn't know the answer? Which steps does a person approve before anything goes out? Does it work with the tools we already use, or do we need new software? Where is our data stored and processed, and is it used for training? Who owns the setup and the logins, and what happens if we stop paying? Can we try it on our own real work before committing? Be wary of anyone who can't answer these in plain words, or who promises AI will run your business for you.
docs.x: AI for small business in New Zealand

docs.t: AI for small business in New Zealand: Where to start with AI in your business
docs.a: Back to that builder at nine o'clock at night. The useful question isn't "how do I use AI?" It's "which part of my week could a good first draft take off me?" Answer that for one task, time it, try it and check it, and you'll know far more than any article can tell you. If you'd like help working out which task fits, that's what our free session is for. We sit with whoever does the work, look at where AI would genuinely help and where plain automation or nothing at all is the better answer, and leave you with a written plan and an hours estimate that's yours to keep. See our AI automation service for how we work.

docs.t: Client portals for small business
docs.a: A client portal gives your customers one private place to send documents, approve work and see where things stand, instead of a trail of emails. It isn't right for every business. This guide helps you decide, and shows what to put in one if you go ahead. A client portal is a private, logged-in area where each customer sees only their own jobs, documents, approvals and invoices. It's usually worth it when you chase the same documents, approvals or updates from many customers, again and again. If you have a handful of customers and simple jobs, good email habits and a shared folder may be enough. Start with one feature, such as document uploads or approvals, and add more once people use it. Treat it as a store of personal information: separate logins, the right permissions, known hosting and a plan for old records.
docs.x: Client portals for small business Digital tools When a portal beats email, what to put in it, and how to keep it secure.

docs.t: Do I need a client portal?
docs.q: Do I need a client portal?
docs.a: Not always. A portal tends to pay off when you exchange documents, approvals or updates with many customers, the same way, week after week, and things get lost in email. If you have a few customers and simple jobs, tidy email and a shared folder may do the job.
docs.x: Client portals for small business

docs.t: What is the difference between a client portal and a customer portal?
docs.q: What is the difference between a client portal and a customer portal?
docs.a: Usually nothing. Advisers and accountants tend to say client portal, while shops, trades and transport businesses often say customer portal. Both mean a private area where each customer signs in and sees only their own information. A staff portal is the same idea for your team.

docs.t: Will my customers need to download an app?
docs.q: Will my customers need to download an app?
docs.a: Usually not. A portal can run in the phone's web browser and be added to the home screen so it feels like an app, without anything to download from an app store.

docs.t: Is a client portal more secure than email?
docs.q: Is a client portal more secure than email?
docs.a: It can be. A portal lets you control who sees what, keep documents in one place and see who approved what and when, rather than having copies spread across inboxes. It still needs good basics, such as separate logins, sensible permissions and two-factor authentication for anyone with wide access.

docs.t: Can a client portal connect to Xero?
docs.q: Can a client portal connect to Xero?
docs.a: It can be set up to show customers what they owe and what they have paid, pulled from your accounting software, and an approval in the portal can create a draft invoice. What is possible depends on the tools involved, so check this before you start.

docs.t: Client portals for small business: What a client portal is
docs.a: Picture an accountant's inbox in tax season. One client has sent bank statements as photos, another has replied to the wrong email thread, and a third has sent the same document twice with different names. Somewhere in there is a signed form, probably. Hi, did you get the statements I sent last week? Not sure if they came through. Attached again just in case. Also what else do you need from me? Those messages are a sign of the problem a client portal solves. A portal is a private, logged-in area of a website. Each customer signs in and sees only what relates to them: their documents, their jobs, what's still outstanding, what they've approved and what they owe. You may hear it called a client portal, a customer portal or a member area. When it's for your team rather than your customers, it's usually called a staff portal. The idea is the same: one place for the things that otherwise get scattered across email, texts and group chats. A portal can work on any phone. It can run in the web browser and be added to the home screen like an app, so nobody has to download anything from an app store.
docs.x: Client portals for small business

docs.t: Client portals for small business: Do you need a client portal?
docs.a: A portal is a tool, not a badge of a modern business. Some businesses get a lot from one. Others would be adding a login nobody uses. This comparison is a good starting point: Email and a shared folder are often enough when A portal is usually worth a look when You have a small number of customers at any time. You work with many customers at once, each at a different stage. Each job needs one or two documents. You chase the same set of documents from every customer. Approvals are rare and simple. Quotes, variations or sign-offs need a clear record of who approved what and when. Customers rarely ask "where's my job up to?". Status questions arrive every day by phone and email. Information is low risk. You handle personal, financial or health details you'd rather not have sitting in inboxes. If most of your answers sit in the right-hand column, a portal could save real time. If they're mostly on the left, start by tidying how email and folders are used. That costs little and may solve most of the problem. Count before you decide. For one normal week, note every time someone chases a document, sends a status update or asks "did you get my email?". That tally tells you more than any feature list. Our guide on choosing what to automate first explains how to time a task.

docs.t: Client portals for small business: When email is still the better choice
docs.a: It's worth being honest about this. A portal asks every customer to do something new: sign in, find their way around and come back next time. If a customer only deals with you once a year, they may forget how. If your customers are mostly older or not confident online, a portal can feel like a barrier rather than a help. Email also has real strengths. Everyone has it, it needs no training and it already sits on every phone. Some simple habits get you a long way: One shared business inbox, rather than documents landing in personal accounts. A standard checklist email that lists exactly what each customer needs to send. A consistent way of naming and filing documents as they arrive. Automatic, polite reminders until everything is in. That last one can be automated without a portal at all. Many businesses start with automated reminders and add a portal later, once they can see where email still falls short.
docs.x: Client portals for small business

docs.t: Client portals for small business: What goes in a client portal
docs.a: The best portals do a few jobs well rather than everything at once. These are the features small businesses most often start with: Document uploads Advisers and accountants Clients upload documents to one safe place, see what's still outstanding and sign forms, instead of emailing attachments. Approvals Trades and building Quotes, variations and sign-offs approved with one tap, with a record of who approved what and when. Invoices and statements Any business that bills Customers see what they owe and what they've paid, pulled from your accounting software. Bookings and tracking Transport and delivery Regular customers book deliveries, track status and download proof of delivery themselves. Other common features include progress photos for a building job, intake forms and upcoming appointments for a clinic, and notes the business wants a client to read on their file. Our industry pages show how portals fit different kinds of work, from advisers and accountants and clinics and salons to trades and building and transport and delivery . Things to leave out at first. Live chat, discussion boards, detailed reports and long settings pages can all wait. Each extra screen is something to build, explain and keep up to date. If customers ask for more once they're using the portal, that's a good sign, and a much better guide than guessing up front.
docs.x: Client portals for small business

docs.t: Client portals for small business: Customer portals and staff portals
docs.a: Many businesses find the same thinking applies on the inside. A staff portal gives your team one place for the day's jobs, notes, photos, checklists and rosters, instead of a group chat. The two often work best together. A building crew uploads photos against a job in the staff portal, and the client sees progress and approves a variation in the customer portal. Because both read from the same records, nobody has to forward photos or retype approvals. If you're unsure which to start with, ask where the most chasing happens. If it's with customers, start there. If it's within your own team, a staff portal may give you more time back first.
docs.x: Client portals for small business

docs.t: Client portals for small business: Connecting a portal to the tools you already use
docs.a: A portal is most useful when it's joined up with the rest of the business, so information is entered once and used everywhere. For example: A job approved in the portal creates a draft invoice in your accounting software, such as Xero. Documents uploaded by a client are filed into the right folder, such as in OneDrive, SharePoint or Google Drive. A completed checklist updates the customer's record, so the reminders stop on their own. The portal's jobs and approvals feed a dashboard, so you can see what's waiting without opening every file. What's possible depends on the tools involved and how they connect. Our guide to connecting your business apps explains how information moves between systems and where it can go wrong.

docs.t: Client portals for small business: Client portal security and privacy
docs.a: General information, not legal advice. For anything specific to your business, check the guidance from the Office of the Privacy Commissioner or talk to a lawyer. A client portal usually holds personal information: names, contact details, and often financial, health or identity documents. Under the Privacy Act 2020 you're expected to keep personal information reasonably safe from loss, misuse and unauthorised access, and what's reasonable depends on how sensitive it is. A well set up portal can be safer than email, because documents live in one controlled place rather than as copies in several inboxes. But only if the basics are right: Separate logins for everyone. Each customer and each staff member has their own, so access can be removed when someone leaves or a job ends. Permissions that match the role. Each customer sees only their own information. Staff see only what their role needs. Two-factor authentication for wide access. At the very least for you and anyone on your team who can see many customers' details. Know where it's hosted. Find out where the portal's data is stored, and who at the provider can see it. A plan for old records. Decide how long documents are kept, and remember copies in other places. Businesses generally need to keep business records for seven years for tax purposes, and your accountant can tell you which records that covers. Test that one customer can't see another's files. Check it before launch, and again after any change. If something does go wrong, such as a document shown to the wrong customer, and it has caused or is likely to cause serious harm, the Privacy Act requires you to notify the Privacy Commissioner and the people affected as soon as practicable. Our guide to the Privacy Act 2020 and automation covers this and has a checklist to run through. When we build portals, they're set up so each person sees only what they should, and you control who has access. Data we store for you is hosted in New Zealand or Australia, and only Ambs works on your project and sees your data.

docs.t: Client portals for small business: What makes customers actually use a portal
docs.a: A portal nobody opens is just another login. The ones that get used tend to share a few traits: It works well on a phone. Many customers will only ever open it on one. Signing in is simple. Fewer steps mean fewer "I can't get in" calls, while still keeping it secure. It saves the customer effort too. Uploading a photo of a document, or approving a quote with one tap, should be easier than finding the right email. Notifications bring people back. A short email or text with a link, such as "your quote is ready to approve", is usually what gets someone to open it. It looks like you. Your logo and colours reassure customers that they're in the right place. Your team uses it consistently. If staff still send documents by email "just this once", customers will too. If many of your customers are more comfortable in another language, it helps if the key screens and messages are in that language too. Have translations checked by a fluent speaker.

docs.t: Client portals for small business: How to start a client portal: one feature first
docs.a: Pick the one job that causes the most chasing. Often it's document collection, approvals or status updates. Write down what done looks like. For example: "clients see their checklist, upload each document against it, and we're told when everything is in.". Decide who can see what. Before anything is built, list the people who'll use it and what each needs to see. Try it with a few friendly customers. Watch where they get stuck and fix that before you invite everyone. Make it the normal way. Point every request to the portal, and stop accepting the same thing three different ways. Add the next feature once it's used. Let real use, not a wish list, decide what comes next.

docs.t: Client portals for small business: Questions to ask before you build or buy a portal
docs.a: Which job will it take off us first, and how much time does that job take now? Who owns the portal, the data and the logins? Where is the data stored, and who can see it? Can each customer only ever see their own information, and how is that tested? Does it connect to the tools we already use, such as our accounting software and file storage? Can customers use it on a phone without downloading an app? Can we export our data and keep everything if we change provider? Who do we call when a customer can't sign in? If you'd like a second opinion on whether a portal is worth it for your business, or which feature to start with, that's what our free session is for. docs.t: AI automation and websites for Auckland businesses: Running a small business in Auckland
docs.a: Auckland is New Zealand's largest city, and most of the businesses that keep it going are small. A café with a handful of staff. A builder with one crew. A clinic where the front desk is often the owner, between clients. A dairy that is open long hours. The work is different in each one, but the admin looks surprisingly similar. Quotes get written at night. Invoices sit as drafts. Reminders go out when someone remembers. The same job is typed into two or three systems. And customers who would rather talk in Chinese, Hindi or Punjabi have to make do with English. We are based in Auckland and work with businesses right across New Zealand. This page covers what that looks like for Auckland businesses in particular: the tasks owners here usually hand off first, how language fits in, what a good local website needs, and how working with us runs from the first conversation.

docs.t: AI automation and websites for Auckland businesses: What Auckland businesses usually hand off first
docs.a: You do not need to automate everything. Most owners start with one task that eats hours every week and follows the same steps every time. These are the tasks we most often suggest taking off first, by type of business: Trades and building: quotes written up from site notes, job invoices into your accounts, and chasing late payments. See our trades and building page . Cafés and takeaways: rosters and shift swap messages, supplier orders and invoice entry, and replies to Google reviews and emails. See our cafés and takeaways page . Clinics and salons: booking reminders and rebooking, new client forms and files, and missed call follow-ups. See our clinics and salons page . Shops and dairies: stock counts and reorders, price and listing updates, and a daily sales summary. See our shops and dairies page . Advisers and accountants: chasing client documents, file notes written from calls, and compliance records and checklists. See our advisers and accountants page . Transport and delivery: run sheets and driver messages, filing proof of delivery, and fuel and mileage logs. See our transport and delivery page . Our typical estimates for the top three tasks in these industries range from about six and a half to nine hours a week. Those are estimates from typical New Zealand jobs, not results. We measure your own week in the free session. Start with the boring work. The best first task is repetitive, rule-based and happens every week. It is not always the job you dislike most. Our guide on how to choose what to automate first gives you a simple way to score your options.

docs.t: AI automation and websites for Auckland businesses: Customers who speak many languages
docs.a: Auckland is home to people from all over the world, and many languages are spoken here every day. Plenty of people feel more confident booking a service or asking about prices in their first language. A business that can answer them in that language builds trust quickly. That is why our own website runs in English, Chinese, Hindi, te reo Māori and Punjabi, and why we speak with customers in English, Hindi and Punjabi. We know the work involved in keeping each version accurate and up to date. Language can help your business in three places: Your website. You do not need to translate the whole site at once. Start with the pages that lead to an enquiry: your services, how pricing works, opening hours and contact details. Have translations checked by a fluent speaker, and let people switch language easily from every page. Customer replies. AI can usually recognise the language a message is written in and reply in the same one, using your approved English answers as the source. So a customer who writes in Chinese, Hindi or Punjabi can get an answer in that language, without you keeping a separate library for each. Anything it is unsure about goes to a person. Reminders and messages. Booking confirmations and reminders can be set up in the languages your customers prefer. Language matters inside the business too. When an automation goes live, we train your team in English, Hindi or Punjabi, whichever they prefer. One honest tip: if you offer a service in another language, say so clearly, and make sure someone can actually reply in it. Our guide to AI customer replies for small business explains how this works and where a person should stay in the loop.

docs.t: AI automation and websites for Auckland businesses: Small business websites for Auckland
docs.a: When someone in Auckland needs a plumber, a physio or an accountant, they usually search on their phone, often on mobile data. They want to know three things quickly: do you do this, do you work near me, and how do I reach you? A website that answers those clearly will usually do more for you than one with beautiful pictures and a vague headline. For a local business, the basics that tend to matter most are: Say what you do and where. "Plumber in West Auckland, same-day callouts" beats "Excellence in every drop". Name the suburbs, city or region you cover, so people know you will come to them. Fast on a phone. Pages should load quickly, text should be readable without zooming, and your phone number should be one tap away. Forms that actually reach you. Each enquiry saved somewhere first, a confirmation sent to the customer, and a notification to the right person. Local search basics. A complete Google Business Profile, the same name, address and phone number everywhere you are listed, a clear title and description for each page, and a page for each main service. Honest trust signals. Your real name, where you are based, photos of your actual work and genuine reviews. Never fake reviews or badges. Nobody can honestly promise first place on Google, and local search tends to build over months. We get the basics right so you have a fair chance. Our guide to websites that turn visitors into calls covers each of these in more depth. A website can also do more than sit there. A chatbot can answer common questions from information you have approved, day or night, and pass anything else to you. A website enquiry can create a customer record and a follow-up task. And a staff or customer portal can put job tracking, photos, invoices and approvals in one place on every phone. More detail is on our websites, portals and dashboards page.

docs.t: AI automation and websites for Auckland businesses: AI automation on the tools you already use
docs.a: Business automation means a system does a task a person used to do by hand, the same way every time. An approved job turns into an invoice. A booking triggers a reminder text. AI is the part that copes with messy input, like a rushed voice memo from a building site or a customer question phrased oddly. You usually do not need new software. We connect the tools most small businesses already pay for: Microsoft 365: Outlook, Excel, Teams, OneDrive and SharePoint. Google Workspace: Gmail, Google Calendar, Google Sheets and Google Drive. Xero for invoices, bills and payments. If you also use a point-of-sale, booking or job management system, we do not connect to it directly. Where it can export to Excel or Google Sheets, or sends you emails, we work from what it already produces. We will tell you honestly in the free session if that is not enough for what you want. AI drafts, people decide. Wherever money, health information or a customer complaint is involved, we set things up so AI prepares the work and a person approves it. Read more on our AI automation page, or see how apps can share information in our guide to connecting your business apps .

docs.a: Information you give us. Your name, business name, email address, phone number and anything you write in our contact form or tell us during an enquiry or engagement. Website preferences. Your chosen language and light or dark display mode, kept on your device for the current browser session only. They are not sent to us and are cleared when you close the browser. Contact form. We do not store this, although those services may keep their own logs. We never ask for or use GPS location. Client data during a project.
